comparison: Strong agreement on thermophilization findings. Both affirm the colonization-extinction dynamics driven by thermal affinity (C55-C63). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation while peer reviewers confirm the evidence is 'convincing' and conclusions are 'sound and well supported.' Both evaluate these core findings as SUPPORTED.

Both support differential CTI responses (C50-C52, C77-C78). OpenEval emphasizes the methodological distinction between abundance-based and occurrence-based CTI, while peer reviewers confirm thermophilization was 'more pronounced for the CTI based on abundances.' Both find this SUPPORTED.

Both affirm the primary study findings (C5-C8, C71). OpenEval notes these integrate multiple lines of evidence into coherent conclusions, while peer reviewers describe the evidence as 'convincing' using 'appropriate and validated methodologies.' Both evaluate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on isolation effects for dispersal limitation (C64-C66, C72-C73). OpenEval highlights the remarkable consistency across species (15/15 warm-adapted, 21/23 cold-adapted), while peer reviewers confirm findings were 'stronger on islands closer to the mainland, due to closer sources to species populations.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both support isolation effects on cold-adapted species extinction (C66, C73). OpenEval emphasizes the multi-species occupancy model accounting for imperfect detection, while peer reviewers attribute patterns to 'limited dispersal (i.e. range shift potential) in more isolated islands.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both address colonization of warm-adapted species (C6). OpenEval integrates this into primary findings with appropriate caution about mechanisms, while peer reviewers specifically confirm the increase of warm-adapted species on less isolated islands. Both SUPPORTED.

Both support extinction patterns of cold-adapted species (C7). OpenEval frames this as part of the integrated primary findings, while peer reviewers explicitly confirm 'decrease of cold-adapted species' was stronger on less isolated islands. Both SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on island area effects and microclimate buffering (C67-C70). OpenEval notes the complexity and empirical temperature support (C96), while peer reviewers confirm warm-adapted species increased more on smaller islands 'due to lowered thermal buffering.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both affirm the empirical temperature monitoring evidence (C96-C97). OpenEval notes this provides direct mechanistic support despite being collected in only one year (2022) on 20 islands, while peer reviewers acknowledge it as important support for thermal buffering hypothesis. Both SUPPORTED.

Both address the mixed patterns in area effects (C69-C70). OpenEval notes complexity for cold-adapted species suggesting multiple mechanisms, while peer reviewers acknowledge 'Island area, in contrast, had a more mixed role in moderating colonization/extinction rates across species.' Both SUPPORTED with appropriate acknowledgment of complexity.

Both support the mechanistic interpretations (C8, C95). OpenEval notes appropriate caution in identifying dispersal limitation and microclimate buffering as 'primary proxies,' while peer reviewers affirm authors 'present interesting mechanisms without being too bold on their findings.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both address dispersal limitation mechanisms (C95). OpenEval provides detailed species-level evidence (15/15 and 21/23 patterns), while peer reviewers affirm the interpretation of dispersal limitation effects. Both SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on study design and methodology (C3-C4, C110-C120). OpenEval details the methodological documentation and sampling protocols, while peer reviewers praise 'extensive bird monitoring data (9 surveys per year per island) across 36 islands' and describe methodologies as 'appropriate and validated.' Both SUPPORTED.

Both affirm the climate warming context (C40, C121). OpenEval notes the significant warming trend is statistically supported with appropriate metrics, while peer reviewers confirm the study covers a period of 'consistent climatic warming.' Both SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on statistical methodology (C130-C135). OpenEval details the MSOM approach for imperfect detection and Bayesian validation (C132), while peer reviewers affirm 'extensive modeling frameworks' and 'appropriate and validated methodologies.' Both SUPPORTED.

Divergence on island isolation metric (C111). OpenEval finds the methodology well-documented and SUPPORTED, while peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, noting the metric 'seems a bit too oversimplified' but acknowledge authors found a signal supporting their method. Different evaluation types (SUPPORTED vs UNCERTAIN).

OpenEval evaluates STI methodology and its lack of correlation with ecological traits (C41-C49, C122-C127) as SUPPORTED with appropriate robustness checks. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the STI metric or its validation.

OpenEval supports the inference about within-region dynamics (C80) and STI as vulnerability indicator (C82-C83) based on strong relationships in the data. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific interpretations about STI and vulnerability.

OpenEval affirms the acknowledgment of heterogeneity in species responses (C93-C94) as SUPPORTED, noting this demonstrates appropriate scientific caution. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this nuanced observation about variation.

OpenEval evaluates conservation recommendations (C101-C103) as SUPPORTED but notes they are inferences about management implications rather than direct empirical results. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific conservation recommendations.

OpenEval rates a priori hypotheses about mechanisms (C25-C26, C32, C36-C37) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are expectations illustrated in Figure 1 rather than empirical findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation distinguishes these hypotheses from results.

OpenEval rates speculative predictions about future trends (C88-C90) as UNCERTAIN, noting they extend beyond the 10-year study period and lack empirical validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these future predictions.

OpenEval rates post-hoc speculation about predation effects (C100) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is explicitly acknowledged as speculation without direct data. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses this speculative mechanism for unexpected patterns.
